items.def: Example: slightly modified versions of legitimate inputs (perturbations often imperceptible to humans) that cause the model to misclassify. Attack: the deliberate use of adversarial examples to cause an ML model to fail.

MT: new (follow-up) test cases are derived from a previously passed source test case by changing it using a metamorphic relation. MR: based on a property of a required function, describes how a change in a test case's inputs is reflected in its expected results.
A change in the distribution of input data over time, which can negatively impact the functional performance of an operational ML model (e.g., spam filter meets new phishing attack types).

A change in the perceived functional performance of an ML model over time caused by changes in user expectations, behavior and the operational environment — the relationship between input and correct output changes (e.g., new regulations reclassify a transaction from low- to high-risk).

The generation of an ML model that corresponds too closely to the training dataset, resulting in a model that finds it difficult to generalize to new data. Detected: performs significantly worse on the separate test dataset than on validation.

The generation of an ML model that does not reflect the underlying trend of the training dataset, resulting in a model that makes inaccurate predictions. Detected: metrics consistently low on BOTH training and validation sets; learning-curve errors remain high and close together.

An approach where the response of two variants of the program (A and B) to the same inputs are compared to determine which variant is better; a statistical approach typically requiring multiple test runs.

Uses an alternative version of the system as a reference point (a pseudo-oracle) and compares its outputs with the system being tested on the same inputs; only test inputs are needed, not expected results.

blocks.title: Documentation, statistics, adversarial, metamorphic, drift, fitting

items.text: Model documentation matters because machine-generated code has limited understandability and models are black-box, data-dependent, frequently updated — documentation is the main tool for developers, testers, regulators (EU AI Act transparency obligations; documentation audit often a deployment prerequisite for high-risk systems). Frameworks: Model Cards (intended uses, evaluation results, ethical considerations), Datasheets for Datasets (motivation, composition, collection, uses). Documentation checklists cover General / Design / Usage / Datasets / Testing / Functional / Non-Functional / Operational; review aims: find missing info, inaccuracies, inconsistencies; improve clarity and maintainability; inform test & deployment; verify regulatory compliance.

Statistical ML functional performance testing: precondition = statistical acceptance criteria, e.g. "98% accuracy with MoE ±4% at 95% CL" (601 test cases; ≥589 pass; sequential testing can stop early ~170 cases if accuracy stays ≥98%; safety-critical example: 99% reliability at 95% confidence → 299 cases all passing). Fix CL → MoE shrinks with more tests; fix MoE → CL grows. Requires a large test dataset completely independent of training/validation and representative of the operational input domain; results reported as e.g. "accuracy of 94% ±4% at the 95% CL", not a passed/failed ratio. (Formulae not examinable — illustration only.)

Adversarial testing: craft perturbed inputs to force misclassification (adversarial examples); enables safeguards. Black-box route: build an equivalent model with known internals, craft inputs there, rely on transferability (equivalent models share classification boundaries) — or brute force random tests. White-box: knowing internals (architecture, parameters, training process) makes crafting easier. Manual crafting or automated generation of large numbers of variations.

Metamorphic testing: verify objectives like consistency, monotonicity, invariance — relationships between outputs instead of absolute values; chosen when no reliable expected outputs exist, system is a black box, or relational properties suffice. MRs come from domain knowledge, requirements, or domain properties (e.g., laws of physics); validate by expert review, reference models, edge-case coverage. Limits: wrong/incomplete MRs → false confidence; MT detects relational flaws, not all absolute errors — combine with other techniques. Example: age-at-death prediction should decrease as cigarettes smoked increase (monotonicity).

Drift testing: dynamic = needs user feedback as current ground truth (direct: user rates a recommendation; indirect: data on films actually watched), compare ground truth vs model output against a threshold; static = no ground truth needed, compares statistical properties of input and predicted-output distributions (e.g., Kolmogorov-Smirnov) — significant difference signals drift.

Overfitting vs underfitting detection (during training, evaluation, tuning): overfitting = good training/validation performance but significantly worse on separate test data including less common examples; underfitting = poor metrics on BOTH training and validation; learning curves: high, close-together, non-improving errors indicate underfitting. Summary: evaluate on validation data, analyze performance metrics, examine learning curves.

A/B testing for MLS: compare two variants on the same inputs to decide which is better (existing system as partial oracle; generates no test cases; operational inputs often incorporated); used for updates with agreed acceptance criteria (updated variant must perform ≥ previous), self-learning systems (accept change or revert). Popular statistical techniques: t-test, z-test, chi-squared, Mann-Whitney U.

Back-to-back testing: pseudo-oracle ideally shares no common software components with the SUT (same defect in both → matching wrong outputs; risky with reusable open-source AI components), ideally built by an independent team with different frameworks/algorithms/settings; conventional software can serve if it solves the same problem; pseudo-oracle needs to match only functional behavior (cheaper). Value: environment migration (dev→prod), comparing results across environments, subtle defects on edge cases. A/B compares variants of the SAME system using performance metrics; back-to-back detects defects.

items.text: A/B: two variants of the SAME system, statistical performance comparison, decides which is better. Back-to-back: alternative system version as pseudo-oracle, same inputs, detects defects; needs no expected results. Metamorphic: follow-up cases from a source case via an MR; checks relationships between outputs. All three address the test oracle problem.

Data drift = input distribution changes (user behavior shifts, seasonality, new phishing patterns). Concept drift = the input→output relationship changes (meaning of data changes; decision boundaries outdated, e.g., regulation reclassifies transactions).

Dynamic needs user feedback as current ground truth (direct ratings or indirect behavior), compared to model output against a threshold. Static needs no ground truth — compares statistical properties of input and predicted-output distributions (Kolmogorov-Smirnov).

Overfit: training/validation good, test set significantly worse. Underfit: poor on BOTH training and validation; learning curves high and close together without improvement. Third outcome: right-fitting.
As test count grows: fix the confidence level → margin of error decreases (more precise); fix the MoE → confidence level increases (more certain).

Black-box adversarial testing crafts inputs on an equivalent model with known internals and applies them to the original model on the assumption that equivalent models share classification boundaries — that assumption is transferability.
